title: Take-Home Assignment Strategy
summary: Approaching a multi-hour or multi-day take-home so effort matches signal — reading what's actually graded before you time-box the work.

slides.markdown:
A take-home swaps the pressure of a live interview for a different trap: unlimited time with no one watching you work. Candidates who'd crush a whiteboard round routinely lose take-homes by spending three days polishing a toy problem, or two hours guessing at ambiguous requirements.

The skill being tested isn't "can you code" — you already cleared that bar to get the assignment. It's **can you manage scope and time like an engineer would on a real ticket.** This topic covers reading the prompt for what's graded, time-boxing before you type, and deciding what to build versus what to explicitly defer.

slides.sectionTitle: Why take-homes are graded on judgment, not just a working solution
slides.markdown:
A live coding round has an interviewer watching every decision in real time — how you approach ambiguity, what you ask, where you get stuck. A take-home strips that out, so the **artifact itself** has to carry all of that signal.

That changes what's actually being scored. A working solution is table stakes; the differentiator is the judgment visible in the code and the README — what you prioritized, what you cut, whether your tests cover the risky paths or just the happy one. Two submissions that both pass the grading script can score very differently once a human reads them.

Treat the take-home as a **sample of how you'd handle a real ticket** with a deadline and unclear requirements, not as a puzzle to solve.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading the prompt for explicit and implicit grading criteria
slides.markdown:
Every take-home prompt has two layers of criteria. The **explicit** layer is what it says outright: "implement endpoints X and Y," "handle these edge cases," "include tests." The **implicit** layer is what it signals without stating it: a prompt that gives you a messy seed dataset is quietly testing data validation; one that mentions "this will run in production" is testing whether you add logging and error handling unprompted.

Before writing anything, reread the prompt once specifically hunting for implicit signals — repeated words, throwaway phrases like "as you see fit," and anything mentioned once but never elaborated on. Those are usually the exact judgment calls being graded.

If a company provides a rubric or scoring guide, treat it as ground truth over your own instincts about what "good code" looks like.

slides.sectionTitle: Time-boxing before you write a single line of code
slides.markdown:
Set your time budget **before** you open an editor, not after you've already sunk two hours. Take the suggested time (or your own honest estimate if none is given), split it roughly into thirds: understanding and planning, building the core, then polish and documentation — and write those numbers down somewhere you'll actually see them.

The planning third feels like it's stealing time from coding, but it's what prevents the single most common failure: building the wrong thing well. Ten minutes sketching what you'll build and explicitly what you won't is cheaper than an hour of code you throw away after realizing you misread the prompt.

Set an actual timer for the polish phase too — it's the phase people blow through when the code "almost works," and it's exactly the phase evaluators notice most (README, tests, edge cases).

slides.sectionTitle: Deciding what to build vs explicitly deferring with a note
slides.markdown:
You will not have time to build everything a production version of this feature would need — and evaluators know that. What separates a strong submission isn't doing more, it's **naming what you didn't do and why**.

A line like "I didn't add rate limiting here — with more time I'd add a token-bucket limiter per API key, since this is the endpoint most exposed to abuse" reads as senior judgment, not a gap. It shows you know the missing piece exists and can reason about it, which is often worth more than the code itself.

Deferring silently — just not mentioning it — reads as either not noticing the gap or hoping no one asks. Both cost you more than the honest note would.

slides.sectionTitle: The real numbers: how long an evaluator actually spends on your submission
slides.markdown:
Most take-homes get reviewed in **15-30 minutes** by a human who is also doing their regular job — not hours of forensic reading. That single fact should reshape how you spend your own time budget.

A reviewer skimming for 20 minutes reads the README first, scans the diff or file structure for organization, runs the tests if they run at all, and spot-checks two or three interesting code paths — they rarely trace every line. That means your README and top-level structure carry disproportionate weight relative to how long they took you to write, and a subtle bug three functions deep is far less likely to sink you than a missing setup step that stops the reviewer from running anything at all.

Optimize for what a 20-minute skim will actually surface, not for what a line-by-line audit would.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a 3-hour suggested take-home vs an open-ended one
slides.markdown:
The suggested duration changes your strategy more than the problem itself does.

| | 3-hour suggested | Open-ended ("take what you need") |
|---|---|---|
| Scope signal | The company has calibrated effort for you — match it | You calibrate effort yourself, which is part of the test |
| Biggest risk | Over-building past the stated budget | Never stopping, or wildly misjudging what "enough" looks like |
| What to do | Time-box strictly to ~3 hours, defer aggressively | Pick a budget (often 4-8 hours), state it in your README, and hold yourself to it |
| Signal you send | Can you execute inside a tight constraint | Can you set your own reasonable constraint and follow it |

**How to decide:** if no time is suggested, don't default to "as much as it takes" — pick a number, write it in your submission, and treat exceeding it as a finding to reflect on, not a plan.

slides.sectionTitle: When and how to ask a clarifying question before you start
slides.markdown:
If the prompt has a genuine ambiguity that would change your approach — not just a detail you could reasonably guess — it's almost always worth one concise, specific email before you start building. "Should the API return paginated results, or is a full list fine for this dataset size?" signals exactly the instinct a real ticket requires: check before building the wrong thing at scale.

The failure mode isn't asking — it's asking too much, or asking things the prompt already answered, which signals you didn't read carefully. One well-chosen question beats three vague ones, and it's almost always better than silently guessing wrong and building on that guess for hours.

If you can't get a response in time, state your assumption explicitly in the README instead of guessing silently.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-engineering a toy problem for days
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If I add a plugin architecture, a caching layer, and 100% test coverage, they'll see how senior I am."

**Why it's wrong:** a take-home evaluates whether your effort matches the problem's actual scope. Spending three days on a prompt suggested to take four hours doesn't read as diligence — it reads as poor judgment about time and priorities, which is precisely the skill the assignment exists to test. It also delays the loop and can signal you'll gold-plate real tickets the same way.

**Correct model:** match the suggested (or self-declared) time budget, solve the actual problem cleanly, and spend any remaining time on tests and the README rather than speculative extensibility nobody asked for.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior-level nuance: signaling seniority through what you didn't build
slides.markdown:
Junior candidates try to signal seniority by adding more — more abstraction, more configurability, more defensive code. Senior candidates signal it by **subtracting well**: cutting scope precisely, explaining the cut, and leaving the door open for the cut piece without building it.

A staff-level submission often looks smaller than a mid-level one, because it spent its time on the two or three decisions that actually mattered (data model, error handling at the boundary, the one gnarly edge case) instead of spreading effort evenly across everything the prompt touched. Evaluators who review a lot of these submissions notice this pattern quickly — an unnecessarily large diff is itself a mild negative signal, not a neutral one.

The question to ask yourself before submitting: "does every piece of this earn its place, or did I build some of it just because I had the time?"
